title: Why Lagos tastes the way it does

lede.text: Lagos lies in the Algarve, at the far south of mainland Portugal, in a south-facing amphitheatre with over 3000 hours of sun a year. Its white wines are normally delicate and soft, with the aroma and flavour of a warm zone.

chapters.title: At the far south
paras: The Algarve lies at the far south of mainland Portugal. It is a well-defined area with features of its own. The nearby sea and the climate shape them. So do the natural vegetation and a culture marked by long Arab rule.
The Lagos area takes in parts of three municipalities: Aljezur and Vila do Bispo, as well as Lagos itself. Its natural limit in Aljezur is the Odeceixe stream.
In Arab times the Algarve grew vines, and its wine was exported. Quality wine from the Algarve was first recognised in 1980.

fly.label: Odeceixe stream
fly.caption: The Odeceixe stream is the natural limit of the Lagos area in Aljezur.

fly.label: Sagres
fly.caption: Sagres parish, in Vila do Bispo, lies wholly inside the Lagos area.

chapters.title: Hot, dry and sheltered
paras: Three things make the climate markedly Mediterranean. The region lies far to the south. A mountain barrier shelters it from cold northern winds. It also opens like an amphitheatre to the south.
It is hot and dry. It is not very windy, and temperature swings are very small. Sun averages over 3000 hours a year.
The vineyards themselves feel the Atlantic, and winds batter them. So their climate is more humid, with bigger temperature swings. Harvests are generally later in this region.

chapters.title: Stony, poor ground
paras: Vines stand in rougher zones, on stonier and less fertile land. They generally run on a north-south line.
Many soils form on sandstone, including the Silves sandstone. Others are sandy, or podzolised coarse sands. Some are red or yellow Mediterranean soils.
The soils are a large part of what sets Lagos apart, in its quality and its character.

chapters.title: Low vines, red and white
paras: Lagos makes red and white wine. The reds need at least 12% alcohol and the whites at least 11.5%.

Whites run from lemon to straw in colour. Reds are generally light in colour: ruby, turning topaz with age. Once bottled, both must be clear. Only wine still in tank or other bulk may be slightly hazy.
The grape list names thirteen varieties. Whites include Arinto and Moscatel Graudo. Reds include Negra Mole and Touriga Nacional.
Vines must be at least four years from grafting and trained low, at about 30 to 40 cm. Yield is capped at 60 hl per hectare.
A wine needs 60 points or more in the tasting to qualify. A quality designation needs 70 or more, with standout structure and balance.
